questions.scenario: You must compare the mean conversion rate across four landing-page designs. A teammate suggests running a t-test on every pair.
questions.question: Why is one-way ANOVA the better first step?
options: ANOVA compares variances, so it cannot say anything about means.
Pairwise t-tests are invalid for more than two groups and will not run.
Running many pairwise t-tests inflates the overall Type 1 error from multiple comparisons. ANOVA tests all group means at once with a single controlled test.
ANOVA is just a faster t-test with identical assumptions and no benefit.
questions.explanation: Each pairwise t-test carries its own false-positive risk, and six comparisons across four groups compound that risk well above the nominal level. One-way ANOVA asks a single question, are any group means different, with one test that controls the error, after which a post-hoc test identifies which pairs differ.
questions.misconception: The problem with many t-tests is multiple comparisons inflating Type 1 error, which ANOVA sidesteps with one omnibus test.

questions.question: What is the core idea behind how ANOVA detects a difference in means?
options: It compares each group's median to the grand median.
It compares the variance between group means to the variance within groups; a large ratio (the F-statistic) signals real differences.
It measures the correlation between group labels.
It counts how many groups are above average.
questions.explanation: ANOVA partitions total variation into between-group and within-group parts. The F-statistic is the between-group variance over the within-group variance. If groups truly differ, between-group variation dominates and F is large relative to its distribution under the null.
questions.misconception: Despite the name analysis of variance, ANOVA tests whether MEANS differ, using variance as the lens.

questions.question: A one-way ANOVA returns a significant result. What can you conclude, and what is the necessary next step?
options: No further analysis is needed; ANOVA names the different group.
Every group mean differs from every other group mean.
At least one group mean differs from another, but not which ones; a post-hoc test (for example Tukey's HSD) is needed to locate the differences.
The group with the highest mean is significantly best.
questions.explanation: A significant ANOVA is an omnibus result: it says the group means are not all equal, without identifying which pairs differ. A post-hoc test with correction for multiple comparisons, such as Tukey's HSD, pinpoints the specific differences.
questions.misconception: A significant ANOVA does not tell you which groups differ. You need a post-hoc test for that.
